doc.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Studio years and the 1959 Europe tour
title: Free and Easy: the 1959 Quincy Jones Europe tour
summary: The show fails, the band stays in Europe, Quincy runs short of money, and they open for Basie at the Olympia.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah. And um so I was getting a little bored, I mean. And you must remember that in 1959 I went to Europe with the Quincy Jones band. There was a show called “Free and Easy.” We were in costume, it was a remake of St. Louis Woman, sound, uh songs by uh Harold Arlen, score by Quincy Jones and Billy Byers. And uh the show only lasted about six weeks, and then Quincy uh said, you know, the flight’s going home Saturday if you want to go home with a failed show or you want to stay in Europe I’ll try to book it. So to a man we all said, “Yeah, we’ll stay.” I mean, I’m trying to imagine if that would happen today, I mean the first thing the cats would say is “How much is the pay?”

We didn’t say that. We had Clark Terry and Budd Johnson, I mean these guys were established family men and all that and they were willing to stay in Europe on a (hummer???) to stay with Quincy Jones because they wanted to play his music, you know? And Quincy took a bath, you know, he lost a lot of money on that tour. People put him down today because he’s so rich, you know he’s doing so well, but I mean I remember when he was suicidal, lost so much bread. I mean I remember living in Paris, I didn’t have enough money to feed my kids and I called Quincy and I said, “I’m busted man. I don’t have enough to get my kids’ dinner.” He said “Come to town, I’ll give you half of what I have.” He had 300 francs, he gave me 150. I mean, you know, you don’t forget that kind of thing, you know. And, and so I got a chance to get familiar with the European thing. That band was very important. Basie, we opened for Basie at the Olympia Theatre in Paris one of the primary venues for music and Jacques Brel, the “Little Sparrow,” Edith Piaf, and I mean it was a big music room, you know, famous music room. We opened for Basie’s band, and Basie, Basie was kidding, but a little serious, he said, “Quincy, you’re not bringing that band home, are you?” [Both laugh] Because these, Basie’s band would say, man, these guys are good, man. We were good. We didn’t use music stands, we didn’t pull out a sheet. That’s another thing: with Dizzy’s band we never pulled out the music.
